claims.text: A page exists at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ (the target of the 'Provider support policy' link card on the Pulumi support index page).
The Pulumi 'Provider support policy' page describes how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
Pulumi's provider support policy designates certain providers as receiving long-term security updates (the page describes which providers get long-term security updates).

Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes any pending operations currently in progress, then exits and reports the error or failure.
To perform a manual rollback after a failed Pulumi deployment, you revert the code and configuration changes and run `pulumi up` to return infrastructure to its previous state.

Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state declared in the program against the last recorded state to determine what changes to make.

Pulumi's not refreshing automatically before every update is an intentional design decision, because refreshing requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, which adds significant latency especially for large stacks.
Under Pulumi's design philosophy, the program is the source of truth for desired state, and changes made outside of Pulumi are treated as drift that the user decides explicitly how to handle.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of the cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/ has a 'Refreshing state' section explaining refresh behavior in detail.
In Pulumi, a resource's logical name is part of its auto-assigned resource URN, while the physical name is how the resource is known to the cloud provider.
A Pulumi resource's logical name only needs to be unique within a stack, while the physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope (sometimes globally).

Pulumi automatically creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards, so that many logical resources and stacks can be stood up side-by-side without conflict.
Pulumi's auto-naming with random suffixes ensures Pulumi can replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
An auto-named resource's physical name typically looks like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` instead of `my-bucket`.
Pulumi auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis, which gives precise physical names without random suffixes but loses the conflict-avoidance and less-downtime replacement benefits.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has an '#autonaming' section and an '#autonaming-configuration' section (Auto-naming Configuration).
Project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable Pulumi auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
Pulumi provides primitives to store secrets securely in the CLI, the state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` causes the configuration value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
For every stack, Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key used to encrypt that stack's secrets, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.

Because a different encryption key is used for each stack, encrypting the same value in two different stacks yields different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files, so an encrypted value cannot be copied between files with a text editor and must instead be set with `pulumi config set`.

When running a preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret config data; it is plain text during the execution of the deployment and any part of the Pulumi program may access it using the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to determine which resources and parameters are available and to determine the return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
A blog post exists at /blog/pulumiup-native-providers/ about Pulumi native providers.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so when defining Pulumi programs you rarely need to leave your IDE.
Pulumi experimental features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When a Pulumi experimental feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi's policy is to focus on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers Pulumi maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The page /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ exists and lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi-maintained providers (beyond the latest major, and beyond any previous-major security updates for covered providers) receive no patches at all.
The Pulumi Registry lists the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources, and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.
Minor provider versions typically include new resources and features, performance improvements, and bug fixes without introducing breaking changes.
The release notes for each provider release summarize the new capabilities or fixes.
In npm, the tilde operator (e.g. `~1.2.3`) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Provider patch versions are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
Pulumi recommends never being two or more major provider versions behind, because jumping multiple major versions can require a multi-step upgrade.
Pulumi recommends updating providers to the latest minor version on the current major at least quarterly.
Pages exist at /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/ (Pulumi ESC FAQ), /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/ (Pulumi Cloud FAQ), and /docs/support/faq/policies/ (Pulumi Policies FAQ).
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version (N-1) for up to 12 months.
For covered providers, Pulumi's security updates for the previous major version end at the earlier of 12 months or the release of the next major version.
The providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions are AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.

The Pulumi Registry has package pages at /registry/packages/aws/, /registry/packages/azure/, /registry/packages/azure-native/, /registry/packages/azuread/, /registry/packages/command/, /registry/packages/docker-build/, /registry/packages/gcp/, /registry/packages/kubernetes/, /registry/packages/tls/, and /registry/packages/vault/.
The Pulumi provider LTS branch ships High/Critical CVE security patches, including fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
The Pulumi provider LTS branch ships fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch that are needed to ship the security patches.

A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions, new resources or new resource properties, performance improvements, non-security bug fixes, or compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi LTS provider releases remain compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless security fixes require otherwise.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, exactly one long-term support major version exists per covered provider at any time.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, when major version N+1 of a provider ships, it becomes the new N and the old N becomes the new LTS major.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, when N+1 ships the previous long-term support major reaches end of life on the same day, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the long-term support major of a Pulumi provider, only the latest minor version receives patches; earlier minor versions are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are tagged differently from current-major releases in package registries.
Pinning to a specific major version of a Pulumi provider is the recommended practice, and customers pinning to a major version automatically receive patch releases as they ship.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered Pulumi provider is the LTS version, and older majors receive no patches.
N is the latest released major version: if v3 is the newest release, then v3 is N, v2 is N−1, and v1 and earlier are end of life.
The current major (N) of a Pulumi provider is supported until N+1 ships and receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions.
The long-term support phase (N−1) of a Pulumi provider lasts up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships, and ships security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
Pulumi provider versions N−2 and older are end of life, are not supported, and will not receive updates.
The Pulumi support FAQ page at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ has a section on 'What are the best practices for maintaining provider versions'.
Pages exist at /registry/ (Pulumi Registry) and /docs/support/getting-support/ (Getting support).
